current_answer: A real commercial expansion with unevenly supported investment and ownership expectations—not an empty market or an inevitable credit crisis. Paid persistence, purposeful purchases, provider cash, useful older capacity and workable funding mechanisms remain substantive favorable evidence. Completed transactions now strengthen the financial side: CoreWeave’s base IPO mostly funded the company, earlier tenders paid existing holders, and Core Scientific’s refinancing repaid a short bridge. These are genuine capital-recycling outcomes, not proof of misconduct or of self-financing operations. The remaining test is whether accepted service, net customer payment and full costs support the prices and claims borne by continuing owners and creditors. A cheaper component, a protected contract or an earlier seller’s receipt cannot answer all of those questions. What the transaction evidence changes; the full-cost service boundary; completion-to-cash conditions.
summary: Useful AI, a successful investor exit and a sound price for the next investor are different achievements. Real cash can reach owners before the business pays for its whole build-out.
uncertainty: For capital recycling, match the cash actually received to the recipient’s complete costs, retained claim and subsequent funding obligations. Successful post-completion collections and manageable future claims would strengthen the productive account; demonstrably unfunded required uses or poor comparable entry economics would weaken it. Neither a new issue price nor one early exit settles the question. Evidence that would distinguish these paths.
